speaker: Drago Anguelov
title: Inside Waymo's New Foundation Model Powering Self-Driving Cars [Drago Anguelov]
question: In autonomous driving, what makes closing the sim-to-real gap in closed-loop simulation so difficult?
guest: Computer graphics is an approximation, and you have to set a whole bunch of knobs properly—what the sun is like, fog, whether the camera lens is grimy—and accurately place complete asset libraries for every scene you drove, which leaves a sim-to-real gap. The dream for a scalable simulator is to reconstruct the environment directly from our own rich cameras and 3D sensors. Technologies like 3D Gaussian splatting can reconstruct the environment you drove really well, but they don't easily let you augment it, turn day into night, or place new agents—that's where generative models like diffusion come in. On top of that, you need to evolve the scene in response to what you do, because your decisions impact the decisions of others. If you just replay what another agent did when you weren't in front of it, it will naively plow into you. So closing the gap requires combining 3D scene reconstruction, generative augmentation, and learned reactive agents that behave realistically.

points.core: Traditional graphics simulators rely on approximations with countless hard-to-tune environmental parameters.
points.note: Accept: CG rendering approximates reality and requires manually tuning lighting, fog, rain, camera grime, or placing complete 3D asset libraries. Do not credit: generic claims that graphics look fake without explaining the parameter or asset approximation problem.

points.core: Pure 3D scene reconstruction cannot easily generate novel unseen environmental variations.
points.note: Accept: reconstructive methods like Gaussian splatting accurately capture logged scenes but cannot easily alter lighting, weather, or insert new elements without generative models like diffusion. Do not credit: claiming 3D reconstruction cannot render logged scenes accurately.

points.core: Naively replaying logged traffic breaks closed-loop evaluation when the vehicle deviates.
points.note: Accept: non-reactive replayed agents ignore the ego vehicle's counterfactual actions and collide with it, requiring learned reactive agent models. Do not credit: generic mentions of multi-agent complexity without explaining why naive log replay fails.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core difficulty is that in closed-loop simulation the simulator must respond realistically to whatever the driving policy does, not just replay recorded data, so every component has to stay faithful in situations that were never logged.

Three gaps compound. First, sensor realism: rendered camera, lidar and radar data differ subtly from real sensors (lighting, weather, noise, rolling shutter, material reflectance), and neural reconstruction methods such as NeRF or Gaussian splatting degrade once the ego vehicle deviates from the recorded trajectory, producing artifacts in novel views. Second, behavioral realism: other agents must react plausibly to the ego vehicle. Log replay is non-reactive, rule-based agents are too simplistic, and learned agents can drift into unrealistic behavior, and human interaction is inherently multimodal and hard to validate. Third, vehicle dynamics and actuation latency are imperfectly modeled.

Because the loop is closed, small errors accumulate: the policy's actions push the simulation into out-of-distribution states where the simulator is least accurate. Safety-critical rare events, which matter most, are also the least represented in data. Finally, measuring the gap itself is hard, since no real-world ground truth exists for counterfactual scenarios.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Closing the sim-to-real gap in closed-loop autonomous driving simulation is difficult because errors across perception, behavior, and physics compound through continuous feedback. Unlike open-loop log replay, closed-loop testing allows the ego vehicle to deviate from recorded trajectories, immediately entering counterfactual states where ground-truth logs no longer apply. Synthesizing physically accurate, temporally consistent camera, LiDAR, and radar inputs from these unseen viewpoints and altered scene layouts is notoriously hard; even modern neural rendering and generative world models introduce subtle geometric, lighting, or sensor-noise artifacts that skew perception modules. Simultaneously, surrounding road users must react plausibly to the ego vehicle’s actions, requiring agent models that capture nuanced human intent, social negotiation, and rare safety-critical behaviors without becoming overly passive or unrealistically aggressive. Imperfections in vehicle dynamics, tire-road friction, and actuation latency further distort how planned maneuvers execute. Because sensing, prediction, planning, and control form a tight feedback loop, minor inaccuracies in any component trigger covariate shift, pushing simulated states progressively further from real-world distributions at every timestep and making simulated performance difficult to trust for real-world safety validation.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Closed-loop simulation is hard because the vehicle's own actions change what it sees next, so the simulator has to be realistic in several ways at once, and errors compound over time.

The first problem is sensors. When the planner steers off a logged trajectory, the simulator must render camera, lidar and radar data from viewpoints that were never recorded. Neural reconstructions such as NeRFs and 3D Gaussian splatting degrade quickly away from the original path, adding artifacts, and perception stacks trained on real data react unpredictably to them.

The second is other road users. Replayed traffic doesn't respond to what the ego car does, while learned or rule-based agents often behave unrealistically: too passive, too aggressive, or not diverse enough. That distorts interaction-heavy scenarios like merges and unprotected turns.

Third, vehicle dynamics, sensor noise, latency and weather are hard to model faithfully. Small mismatches build up over many steps, and policies can learn to exploit those flaws.

Finally, there's no good way to check fidelity. Simulated and real results often correlate poorly, and the rare long-tail events that matter most are exactly the ones with the least data to model them.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Closing the sim-to-real gap in closed-loop autonomous driving simulation is difficult because small modeling errors compound over time. Unlike open-loop log replay, a closed-loop planner's decisions continuously change its future trajectory, forcing the simulator to generate counterfactual sensor inputs and world states that never occurred in the original recording. Re-synthesizing realistic camera, LiDAR, and radar data from novel viewpoints—complete with accurate lighting, weather, occlusions, reflections, and hardware-specific noise—remains hard without introducing subtle artifacts that perception models can exploit or trip over. Equally challenging is simulating realistic, reactive traffic: surrounding drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians must respond naturally to the ego vehicle's maneuvers, capturing subtle social negotiation and unpredictable human intent rather than following scripted paths. Meanwhile, imperfections in vehicle dynamics, tire friction, and actuation latency cause simulated motion to diverge from physical reality. Together, these sensor, behavioral, and physical discrepancies create distribution shifts that make it difficult to trust whether strong closed-loop simulator performance truly transfers to the real world.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
In closed-loop simulation, every action changes what the vehicle sees next and how other road users may respond. A small mismatch in camera glare, tire grip, or another driver’s reaction can alter the vehicle’s next decision. Over several decisions, those differences can compound until the simulated vehicle is facing a situation quite different from what it would encounter on the road.

Real driving logs help calibrate simulators, but they only record what happened after the actions actually taken. If the simulated vehicle brakes earlier or merges later, the simulator has to predict how nearby drivers and pedestrians would respond. Those responses are especially hard to validate in rare, safety-critical situations, where real-world examples are scarce. A simulator can look realistic and match everyday driving statistics while still giving misleading results about how a driving system handles a near miss.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
In closed-loop simulation, the car’s actions change what it sees next. If it brakes a little later in simulation than it would on the road, it may reach a merge at a different moment, prompting another driver to yield or accelerate. That response changes the car’s next decision, so a small initial mismatch can lead to a very different encounter.

Real-world recordings show what happened after the action the car actually took. They cannot show how the same people would have reacted to a different action. A simulator therefore has to predict those reactions while also reproducing vehicle motion and sensor readings accurately enough to guide the next decision. Validating those predictions is especially difficult in rare, safety-critical situations, where real examples are scarce and small differences in timing can determine the outcome.
